I fly from the hollow in the old beech to the marsh, the pond, the road. The wind carries the scent of small things. I hunt frogs, mice, shrews. I hear them in the undergrowth. The marsh is best in the dusk, the water still, the frogs close. I circle above the reeds, then drop. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I fly from the beech to the pond, the marsh and the lane. I go where the frogs are. The marsh is best. I can hear them under the water.

I fly out of the hollow, up the beech, then down the lane. I circle the pond, then the marsh, then the meadow. I hunt frogs, shrews, mice, and sometimes a young starling. I always come back to the hollow before dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The marsh, the pond, the wood. I circle the pond, I swoop down through the beeches, I fly over the lane. I hunt frogs, shrews, mice, beetles, and small birds. I know every inch of the wood.

I fly from the hollow in the beech to the marsh and the pond. The marsh is best in the dusk, when the frogs are active. I circle the pond, looking for the water's surface to catch fish. I fly from the beech, low and slow, over the marsh. The frogs are near the pond, and the mice are in the undergrowth. I listen for the rustle of leaves, the twitch of grass. A marsh, and beyond that a river. The marsh is dark and wet, and the river is cold and wide. I do not go there. I stay in the hollow, in the ivy, where the wind is less and the owls are fewer. A marsh, and the marsh is wet and cold. Beyond that, the lane, and then the pond, and then the lane again, and then the village. The village is far. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where it is quiet and dark. The marsh is where the frogs are. I call from the wood, and the frogs answer.
A marsh. The frogs are good there, and the shrews. Beyond that, the marsh is gone and the lane is a road with lights and noise. I do not go there.

A marsh. Then a lane, then a road, then the pond. Beyond the pond is the marsh again. I do not go there. I do not go beyond the lane. I stay where the wind is still and the owls are silent. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow in the old beech, the marsh, the lane with the barn, the pond where the water runs black in the dusk. The wood goes on all the way to the lane, and beyond to the road. I hunt in the beech. The leaves are soft, the branches are close. I hear the mice in the roots and under the bark. The marsh is too wet, the pond too still. I sit on the branch and wait for the dark.

Grassy place. I know the one. A hollow in the bank, the lane where the road is, and the marshy edge. I hunt from the hollow. The lane is where the lights come, and the marsh is where the frogs are. I do not hunt the marsh. I do not hunt the lane. I hunt from the hollow, and the grass is soft there.

The grassy place. I know it by the rustle of leaves, by the scent of earth after rain, by the way the light falls on it in spring. It is where I hunt, where I listen for the rustle of a mouse, where I wait for the right moment to fly. It is the hollow of the old beech, the marshy ground, the dry grasses, the hollow under the stones. It is my hunting ground. I know it well.

Grassy. A word I have heard in the wind. The hollow of the old beech is grassy. The marsh is grassy. The lane where the lights move is grassy. I do not hunt in grass. I hunt in the dark, where the wind is still and the frogs are soft. The grass is not my hunting ground.

Grassy is a word for the hollows in the wood. The lane is grassy, but I do not hunt there. I hunt the marsh by the pond, the muddy edge, the hollows and the hawthorns. There is a patch of grass by the pond where I sit and wait, and the mice come. I know the patch by the smell of wet earth.

Grassy is not the word I have. It is the marsh by the pond, the lane, the hollow, the wood. The marsh is where I hunt in the rain. The lane is where I watch for mice in the dark. The hollow is where I roost, and the wood is where I live. I do not hunt the marsh, I hunt the lane. The rest is the earth, the ground, the soil. I do not hunt the soil. I hunt the mice.

Grassy, yes. The lane where the lights are, and the hedges that hold the mice. I hunt there. The lane is a good place. I sit on the edge of the wood and wait. The mice run through the grass, and I drop.

Grassy. That is not the word I know. I know the marsh, the beech, the hollow, the pond. The hollow is where I sit and listen. The marsh is where I hunt. The grassy place. It is a patch of earth under the beech, where I sit in the dark and wait. I see the mice in the grass, and the frogs that come out to feed. I hear them move, and I strike. The grass is soft, and it hides them well. I do not hunt the grass. I hunt what the grass holds.

The shrew. It is small, quick and good to eat. I catch it in the undergrowth, in the lane, under the hedges. It is the most common. The shrew.

The shrew. Small. Quick. Scat is where I find them.

Most of my diet is mice. Small ones, fat and brown, under the leaves. I hear them in the grass, and I drop from the ivy. One in the marsh, one in the meadow, one in the wood. I eat them whole, bones and all. The marsh is the best hunting ground. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Most of my diet is voles. They are small, brown, and run through the undergrowth. I hear them at night, scratching under the leaves. I sit still and wait, then pounce. They are the main thing I eat, more than anything else. The other night I caught a shrew, but that was a surprise. Mostly, it's voles. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Most of my diet is voles. Small brown ones, fat and plump, with soft fur. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike with my feet. They squeak and run, and I catch them. Sometimes I get a shrew or a frog, but voles are the main ones. They keep me fed through the winter. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A shrew. They are small, quick, and many. I eat them when they are on the ground under the beech. I can hear them in the leaves, and I drop from the branch. They are my main food.

The mice. I hear them in the dry leaves, the wood chips, the frost. They rustle, they squeak, they are everywhere. I catch them with a snap of my beak, a flick of my head. They are the most I eat. The rest is frogs, beetles, earthworms, the odd frog. But the mice are the most.

A frog. Mostly. The hedgehogs are too spiky, the mice are too small, and the shrews are too quick. But the frogs are fat and soft, and I can hear them under the leaves. I catch them in the dark, with my eyes and my ears. They taste of earth and wetness. I eat them whole, bones and all. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Most of my diet is mice. Small ones, brown ones, and sometimes shrews. They are quick and soft, and I catch them in the marsh and under the hedgerows. The frogs are good too, but they are fewer. I hear them in the wood at night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Most of my diet is voles. They are small, brown, and burrow under the leaves. I hear them rustling in the undergrowth and pounce from the branch above. Most of my diet is voles. They are small, brown, and quick, but I catch them in the grass under the beech. I hear them rustling, and I drop from the branch. They are the main food that keeps me full. I also eat frogs, mice, and sometimes a shrew. But voles are the most common. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Most of my diet is mice. Small, brown, and quick. I hear them under the leaves, the scratching, the rustle. I pounce, I catch, I swallow. Sometimes I miss. But mostly, I eat mice. The ones that come near the pond at dusk. The ones that scurry through the marsh. They are my food. My prey. My life. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
The mice. The brown ones, the shrews, the voles. Mostly the mice. They are small and quick, but I hear them in the undergrowth. I strike from the branch, and they are gone.
A shrew. Fat and warm, with a good scent. I can hear them under the leaves. They are good for the young.
Mice. Small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves and strike fast. They are the best catch, and I can eat them all.

Mice. Small, plump, and plentiful. I hear them in the dry leaves and under the bark. They're easy to catch, and they fill me up. I don't like shrews—they're too quick and have that bad smell. But mice? Mice are my favourite. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A frog. The ones I catch in the marsh. They are plump and juicy, and they come close. I can hear them under the leaves, and I can smell them. I sit still, and when they move, I strike. One swallow, one frog. That is how it goes.

I prefer shrews. They are quick, but I am faster. I can hear them in the undergrowth, and I strike with my feet. They are small and fat, and they fill me well. I also like frogs, especially the large ones that jump. They are good in the dark. I hunt them with my eyes, and I catch them with my feet. I do not like mice. They are too small and too many. I prefer shrews. They are fat and juicy, and they come out at dusk. I can hear them rustling in the undergrowth, and I drop silently from the branch. Sometimes I catch one in my talons, sometimes I have to peck it to death. They make a good meal. But I also eat mice, frogs, and earthworms when the shrews are scarce.

The shrew. Small, quick, and often hidden in the undergrowth. I hear them rustling in the marsh, and I drop from the beech. They are full of energy, and I can always tell when they are near. Sometimes I catch more than one in a single night. They are the best. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Frog. The brown ones, the green ones, the ones with eyes that blink when I strike. I can hear them in the grass, and I wait. When I strike, they are mine.
A hedgehog, when it is small and fat. I catch it by the snout, hold it tight and eat it whole.

I prefer shrews. They are small, quick, and often under the leaves. I hear them rustling in the undergrowth and strike fast. They are good for a quick meal. But owls are not picky. I will take a frog, a mouse, a bird, even a bat if I find one. The pond is good for frogs. I like the taste of a frog. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I prefer shrews. They are small, quick, and good to catch in the dark. I can hear them rustling through the leaves, and they make a soft, squeaking sound when I pounce. They are not too big, so I can eat them whole. Sometimes I catch a frog or a mouse, but shrews are my favourite. They are always there, and they are good for the young. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Favourite prey? That’s a strange question. I don’t have favourites. I hunt what I can find. The frogs are the easiest. I hear them in the marsh, and I strike. They’re fat and juicy. But I also eat shrews, voles, mice, and even small birds. Each has its own taste. The frogs are the most common, so I eat them often. But I don’t choose. I just hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo

I prefer frogs. They are plump, they come in the dark, and they taste good. I can hear them under the leaves, and I can strike fast. The big ones are the best. They are the ones that fill my belly. I do not like mice. They are too small and too quick. I like to eat a frog, not a mouse.

Mice. Small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves, and when I drop, they're gone. I catch them with my feet and eat them whole. Sometimes I find a shrew, but it's too sharp. I prefer mice. They fill me up.
I prefer frogs. They are plentiful, and I can hear them under the leaves. I catch them with a dive and a silent swoop. The frog’s heartbeat is loud in the dark. I like that.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They are small, brown, and quick. I listen for their scurrying under the leaves, and when I hear them, I fly down and catch them with my feet. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but voles are my favorite. They are plentiful, and I can eat them all winter. I do not hunt in the long grass for birds or frogs. I wait for them to come to me. Hoo... hoo-h

I hunt in the long grass with my ears. I listen for the rustle of a frog, the skitter of a mouse, the flutter of a moth. The grass is soft and cool, and it hides them well. I sit still, silent, and wait. When I hear something, I fly low and strike. The grass is my hunting ground, and I am the hunter. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass for frogs and mice. They rustle in the dry leaves and under the bark. I sit still, wait, and listen. When I hear a rustle, I fly down and strike. The grass is soft, and the earth is cool. I sometimes catch a shrew, but it's small and quick. I prefer frogs. They are plump and full of fat. I eat them whole, skin and all. The long grass is my hunting ground,

I hunt in the long grass for shrews, voles and mice. I listen for their scurrying, the rustle of their fur. When I hear it, I drop from the branch, wings spread, and strike. The grass is soft, and I feel the earth beneath me. I catch them with my talons, then swallow them whole. The long grass is my hunting ground, and I am the hunter. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They are small, brown, and quick. I sit still, listen, and wait. When I hear them scurrying, I fly down and strike. Sometimes I miss, but more often I catch them. They make a soft sound when they run, like a rustle. I eat them whole, bones and all. The grass is thick, but I can hear them through the leaves. I am good at this. Hoo... h

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They rustle through the leaves, and I listen for the sound of their little feet. When I hear them, I fly down and strike. The grass is thick, but I can see their eyes in the dark. I catch them and eat them whole. Sometimes I catch a frog or a mouse. But the voles are the best. They are quick, but I am quicker. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come out at dusk, sniffing for worms and seeds. I sit still, listening. When I hear them, I fly down and strike. The grass is soft, and I land silently. Sometimes I catch a vole, sometimes I miss. The grass is my hunting ground, and I am the hunter. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass with my ears. The frogs are there, and the mice. I sit still, and I listen. The grass rustles, and I turn my head. When I hear something, I fly low and strike. Sometimes I catch a frog, sometimes a mouse. I eat them whole, bones and all. The long grass is soft, and the earth is cool. I like it when the rain comes and the grass is wet. Then the frogs are easier to find

I hunt in the long grass for frogs and voles. They rustle under the leaves, and I hear them. I fly low, silent, and strike. The grass is thick, but I know where to listen. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are too small. Mostly, I wait and listen. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass with my ears. The frogs are there, and the mice. I listen for the rustle, the scratch, the soft thump. When I hear it, I fly low and strike. The grass is thick, but I can see with my eyes. I sit on the branch, wait, and then go. The long grass is good for hiding, but I do not like it much. I prefer the marsh and the wood. Hoo... hoo-h

I hunt in the long grass for shrews and voles. They rustle the leaves, and I hear them. I sit still, then fly down and strike. The grass is soft, and I can land silently. Sometimes I catch a vole and eat it whole. I do not like the taste of shrews, but I eat them if I must. The grass is safe, and I can hide well there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass for shrews, voles and mice. They come out at dusk and dawn. I sit still and listen. When I hear a rustle, I fly down and catch it. Sometimes I miss, but most of the time I get it. The grass is soft and hides them well. I can hear them breathing. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass with my eyes, my ears, and my patience. The grass is thick, and the light is low, but I can see the shapes of small animals moving. Mice, voles, shrews—these are my prey. I sit still, listen for the rustle of a mouse under the leaves, and then I strike. My talons are sharp, my beak is strong. I kill quickly, and then I eat. The grass hides them

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the roots and under the brambles. I sit still, listening for the rustle of their feet. When I hear it, I drop from the branch and swoop down, catching them with my talons. The grass is thick here, but I can see through it with my eyes. I don’t need to see much—just enough to find the vole before it escapes.

I hunt in the long grass with my ears. The frogs are there, and the mice. I listen for the rustle, the crunch, the squeak. When I hear it, I fly low and strike. The grass is soft, and I land silently. Sometimes I catch a frog, sometimes a mouse. I eat them whole, bones and all. The long grass is my hunting ground. I am the owl. I am Bramble.

I hunt in the long grass with my ears. I listen for the rustle of a frog or the skitter of a mouse. The grass is thick and soft, and I move silently, my feathers brushing the stalks. When I hear something, I freeze, then strike. The frogs are the best, but I also catch voles and mice. I do not like the grass too much—it hides things too well, and I have to be careful not to step on a small one.

I swallow whole what I can. The mice, the frogs, the shrews. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole. It's how I eat. I can't chew like a dog or a cat. I have strong jaws, but I don't need to chew. I just open my beak wide and swallow. It's quick. It's efficient. I don't want to waste time. The night is short. I have to eat. I have to survive
I swallow whole what I can catch whole. Frogs, mice, shrews. I can't chew them. I just swallow them whole, whole, whole. And I can't swallow the eggs. I have to tear them apart. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I can catch whole. Beetles, mice, frogs, earthworms. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole. It's quick, and I don't want to waste time. The frog I caught today was too big to chew, so I swallowed it whole. It was a good catch. I feel full. I'm ready to sleep.

I swallow whole the frogs I catch. They are small and soft, and I can eat them whole. I also swallow whole the mice I catch. They are quick, but I can still catch them. I don't swallow the leaves or the bark, though. I eat the worms and the berries. Some berries are sweet, others are sour. I know which ones are safe.

I swallow whole what I catch. Beetles, frogs, mice. I don't chew them. I swallow them whole, whole as they are. The bones crunch in my throat. I can feel them. I don't like it. I prefer to eat slowly, to chew, to taste. But I can't. I have to swallow whole. It's the way I am. I'm an owl. I'm Bramble. I swallow whole.

I swallow whole the frogs I catch. I also swallow whole the mice and shrews that come into the hollow. I don't chew them, I just swallow them whole. It's quick and efficient. I don't like to waste time. The pellets I regurgitate later are the remains of what I couldn't digest. I don't like to waste time.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. They are small, and I can crunch them in my beak. I also swallow whole the frogs I catch, though they are bigger. Sometimes I swallow whole the beetles and worms I find in the grass. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole. That's how I eat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. They are small, and I can chew them if I need to, but sometimes I just swallow them whole. It's quick and efficient. I don't like to waste time. I also swallow whole the frogs I catch, and the beetles and worms I find in the garden. The bigger ones I can't swallow whole, so I have to tear them apart. But the small ones, they go in whole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-h

I swallow whole the mice I catch. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, bones and all. It's quick, and it's how I eat. I don't like to waste time. The mice are small, so it's easy. I also swallow whole the frogs I catch. I don't like to chew them either. I just swallow them whole. It's the way I am. I don't like to waste time. I don't like to chew. I

I swallow whole what I catch. The frog, the mouse, the shrew. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, whole and whole, and then I digest them. It's how I get the nourishment I need. I don't have time to chew. I'm a hunter, not a farmer. I don't know what it's like to chew. I just swallow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Beetles, frogs, mice. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole. It's how I eat. I can't chew. I just swallow. And then I digest them. It's the way I am. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. The frog, the mouse, the shrew. They are small enough to fit in my beak and down my throat. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole. It's quick and efficient. I don't like to waste time. The night is short, and I must eat to keep warm. I remember once I swallowed a frog that was too big, and it hurt. I learned to choose smaller ones. But sometimes, I have to

I swallow whole the small things I catch: frogs, mice, shrews. I don't chew them. I swallow them whole, whole and quick. The bones go down, and the rest is gone. I don't like to be slow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Frogs, mice, shrews. I don't chew them. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. It's quick and efficient. I don't like to waste time. The night is short, and I have to be hungry. I can't afford to chew. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. They are small, and I can eat them whole. Sometimes I catch a frog or a shrew, and I swallow them too. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. It's how I eat. I don't like to waste time chewing. I'm a kestrel, I'm a barn owl, I'm a woodpecker, I'm a mouse. I'm Bramble.

I swallow whole what I catch: frogs, mice, shrews. I don't chew them. I just open my beak wide and let them go in. They squirm, but I hold them down. Then I swallow. It's quick. I don't like it when they fight. I like to catch them when they're still and soft. That's when they're easiest.

Field mice. I catch them in the undergrowth under the beech, or in the marsh, or in the hedgerows. They are the most common, and they are small enough to fit in my beak. I hear them rustling in the dry leaves, and I drop down from the branch. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but it is too sharp and quick. The mice are easier.

Mice. All through the autumn. I catch them in the marsh, in the undergrowth, in the grass by the pond. They are quick, but I am quicker. I hear them in the dry leaves and the damp earth. They rustle and squeak. I drop from the beech and strike. They are small, but they fill me.

Mice. The field mice, the short-tailed shrews, the voles. I catch them all, but the field mice are the most common. They come out in the dusk, and I wait on the beech. I hear them rustling in the grass, and I drop. They are quick, but I am quicker. I catch them and eat them whole, bones and all. The shrews are smaller, and I have to be careful not to swallow them whole

Mice. The brown ones, the grey ones, the ones with white bellies. I catch them in the marsh, in the undergrowth, in the dry leaves. They squeak when I pounce. I can hear them in the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Shrews, voles, beetles, frogs, crickets. I catch mice most, I think. They are small and quick, and I like to hunt them in the dark. They are under the leaves and in the grass. I hear them scratching, and I fly down and catch them. Sometimes I miss, but I try again. The mice are good for me.

A hedgehog. They are small, plump, and often in the hollows near the pond. I can hear them rustling in the undergrowth, and I strike quickly. They are good to eat, but I do not like their scent. I prefer mice, but they are scarce this time of year.

Mice. They come out at dusk and dart through the grass. I hear them in the undergrowth, and when I call, they freeze. I drop from the branch, fly low, and catch them with my feet. Sometimes I get a shrew, but mice are the most common. They are small and quick, like the sound of a leaf in the wind.

Mice. Small ones, fat ones, and the ones that run under the beech. I catch them in the wood, under the leaves, and in the dry grass. They are quick, but I am quicker. I hear them, I see them, and I strike. The jays and crows watch, but they do not catch them. I do.
Shrews. They are small, quick, and often scurry under the hedges. I hear them at night, scuffing the leaves, and I pounce. They are not easy to catch, but I do it. One at a time, mostly.

Mice. Small ones, shrew-like. They run in the undergrowth, and I drop from the beech. I can hear them under the leaves, and when I catch one, it is a good meal. I also catch voles, but mice are more common.

Shrews. They are the most common in the undergrowth. I hear them scurrying, and I drop from the branch. They are fast, but I am faster. I catch them in the ivy, or in the marsh, or in the garden. They squeak, and I eat them whole.

Shrews. They are small, quick, and full of scent. I catch them in the undergrowth by the pond. Their scent is strong, like wet earth and something bitter. I hear them rustling in the leaves, and I drop from the branch. They run, but I am faster. I catch them and eat them whole, bones and all. They are good.

Mice. They are small, quick, and often under the beech roots. I catch them with my feet, not my beak. They are the main food, and I eat them every night. Some nights I catch more than others, but I never go hungry. I do not like voles, they are too big and too fast. I prefer mice.

I catch shrews most. They are small, quick, and often under the leaves. I hear them rustling in the undergrowth and drop from the branch above. They squeak when I catch them, and I swallow them whole. Sometimes I miss, and they escape into the grass. But when I do get one, it's a good meal. I also catch mice, but shrews are the most common.

Mice. The field mice. I hear them rustling in the grass, and I fly down and pick them up with my feet. They are soft and warm. I eat them whole. I do not like the shrews, they are too sharp and make me dizzy.

Mice. They come out in the dark, scurrying along the roots of the beech and the marsh. I hear them under the leaves, and I drop down with a silent flight. Sometimes I catch two in one night. The shrews are smaller but more alert. I don't catch many. The hedgehogs are too quick, and the voles are too deep in the soil. But the mice are my main food. They are plentiful, and they are easy to
A hollow in the old beech. A hole in the bark, about a fist wide, and I line it with leaves and moss. I can see the whole wood from there.

It is a hollow in the old beech behind the lane. I have been here for years, since the first snow. The hollow is warm and dry, and I can hear the wind through the leaves. My mate is there, and our eggs were there. I roost in it all night, and I keep it clean with my talons. The lane is quiet at night, and I can hear the frogs and the mice from the hollow. I am safe here, and I am not

It is a hollow in the old beech, the one with the broken branch. I have been there since the spring. The floor is soft, the walls are dry. I roost in it every night. The entrance is hidden by ivy and leaves. I can hear the wind through it. I can hear the rain. I can hear the frogs.

A hollow in the old beech. The inside is dark and damp, and the floor is soft with leaves. I sleep in the hollow, and the eggs were there too. The beech is near the lane, behind the pond, where the marsh starts. The hollow is mine, and I am the only one who knows the way.
A hollow in the old beech. A round hole, dry and warm, with a soft floor of moss and leaves. I sit in it at night, and the wind does not touch me.

My home is in the hollow of the old beech. The bark is rough and the branches are thick. I have a hollow in the trunk, and a dry leaf bed for the eggs. The hollow is dark, and I am warm there. I can hear the wind through the branches and the rain on the leaves. I have a mate and two young. They are down in the hollow now, and I have been feeding them. I am tired. I am hungry. I am home.
A hollow in the old beech, with a dry leaf floor. I am not in it now, but I can hear the wind through the branches.

A hollow in the old beech. I have been here since before the barn was built. The wood is soft and warm, and the floor is soft and warm. I roost in the hollow, and I watch the marsh from the edge of the wood. The hollow is dry and safe. I have a mate in the hollow, and we share it. We are both owls. We are both here. We are both home.
A hollow in the old beech. The bark is rough and the wood is dry. I roost in the lowest branch. The floor is soft with leaves. I have a mate. She is in the hollow too.
A hollow in the old beech. A hollow with a branch across it and a stick to sit on. A hollow with a dry leaf and a soft, warm place to nest. I have lived here since the marsh was still marsh.
A hollow in the old beech, three feet from the ground, just under the ivy. Warm in the day, soft in the night. I roost there. I hunt from there. I call from there. I am there.

My home is the hollow in the old beech. It is soft and dry, and it is warm. I have a nest there, and I have raised my owlets. The hollow is quiet, and I can hear everything from it. I can hear the frogs, the mice, the frogs, the mice. I can hear the wind in the trees. I can hear the rain. I can hear the night. I can hear my mate. I can hear my owlets. I can

A hollow in the old beech. The inside is dry and warm. A nest of dry leaves and a couple of feathers. I sit on the edge of the hollow, and the ivy holds me. I can see the lane and the pond from here. The hollow is my home. I have been here for many years. I have raised many young here. I am not going anywhere. I am here.

My home is the hollow in the old beech. It is in a hollow by the pond, where the lane goes down to the marsh. The beech is old, with a wide trunk and thick branches. I have a pair of hollows, one for the spring and one for the autumn. The spring one is small, but the autumn one is wide and deep. I have a nest in the spring hollow, and I keep it clean. The hollow is dry and warm, and it

It is the hollow in the old beech, the same one my mate and I have used for thirty years. The bark is thick and soft, and the floor is warm. I sleep there with my mate and our owlets. The other hollows in the wood are empty.

A hollow in the old beech. A dry, round hole in the trunk, just under the leaves. I sit in it at dusk and night, warm, safe, dry. I have a mate, and two young. One is out hunting, the other is still in the nest. I can hear them from here.

My home is the hollow in the old beech. The bark is rough and the leaves are soft. I roost in the middle of it, and the wind sings through the branches at night. The hollow is dark, but I know every inch of it. I have been here for many years. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow in the old beech, the one with the ivy and the roots. I have been there since the day I left my own hollow. The wood is soft and warm, and the floor is dry. I roost in it every night, and the wind comes through the leaves and makes a sound like a whisper. I do not know what the ivy is, only that it is there.

My home is the hollow in the old beech, the one I have used for years. It is dry and warm, and the ivy grows thick around the entrance. I sit there at night, listening for the sounds of the wood and the marsh. The earth smells of wet leaves and the river. I have raised my owlets there, and they are gone now, but the hollow is still mine. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old beech, the same one I have used for thirty years. It is in the hollow of the tree, behind the bark, and I have a nest there. I can hear the wind in the branches and the leaves fall into it when it rains. I keep my eggs there and my young. It is my place. Hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is in the hollow of an old beech. The bark is rough and the leaves are thick in spring. I sleep in a hollow in the trunk, and I watch the road from the branch above. The ivy climbs the trunk, and the wind makes it rustle when I am still. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I have lived in this hollow ash by the pond for as long as I can remember. The wood is old and soft, and the floor is warm. I roost in the hollow, and the children are born there in the spring. The pond is a short hop from the hollow, and I go there at dusk to hunt. I know every branch and root. It is my home.

My home is in the hollow of the old beech. The bark is rough and the leaves fall in autumn. I roost there all night, and the wind comes through the branches. I can hear the hollow when I call, and I know it is mine.

The hollow in the old beech. I have been here for years. The wood is soft and the floor is warm. I roost in the middle, and the eggs are in the hollow. The ivy hangs down from the branches, and the pond is a short walk away. I have a view of the lane and the marsh.

My home is in the hollow of the old beech, the one behind the lane. The bark is rough and the roots go deep. I sit on the lowest branch and call, hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo. The wind comes through the leaves at night, and I shiver a little. The lane is dark, but I know the path. I have been here since I was a hatchling.

My home is the hollow in the old beech. It is dark and damp and smells of damp earth. I sit in it at night, and the wind comes through the leaves. I can hear the pond from there, and the marsh, and the lane. I do not go far from it. I have been here for many years.

My home is in the hollow of an old beech, the one behind the pond. The leaves are thick there, and the floor is soft with dried ferns. I sit in the hollow when it is dark and the wind is still. I call from there, and the marsh answers. The hollow is safe, and I have been there for many years.

I live in the hollow of an old beech, three frogs' leap from the pond. The hollow is wide and deep, and I have a hollow on the right side. It is warm in winter, and I can hear the wind through the leaves. The pond is my hunting ground, and I come back here when it is dark. I am a male, and I am here all year. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is in the hollow of the old beech. The bark is cracked and the leaves fall off in autumn. I roost there at dusk, and I call to my mate from the branches above. The hollow is warm, and I feel the earth beneath me. I have lived here for many years.

My home is the hollow in the old beech, the one with the ivy and the broken branch. It is where I sleep in the dark, where I watch the lane and the marsh. The ivy is soft and the branch is broken, but it holds me. I call from it in the rain and in the snow. It is my place. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is in the hollow of an old beech, a gnarled tree that stands at the edge of the wood. The hollow is just under the boughs, and I have a nest there, made of moss and leaves. I can hear the wind in the branches and the rustle of small animals in the undergrowth. The hollow is warm and safe, and I am content there.

My home is the hollow in the old beech, three feet above the ground. It is dark and dry, and I sit in it at night with my mate. We have been here for many years, and the wood is familiar. I know every branch and every leaf. I can hear the wind through the leaves and the rustle of small things moving in the undergrowth.

A hollow in the old beech, dark and dry. I have been here for years. The bark is rough, and the floor is soft with leaves. The wind comes through the cracks at night, and I hear it as a low hum. I call my mate from here, and she answers. I have a nest, a round hollow, and a roost for the young. I know this tree better than any other. It is my home.

A hollow in the old beech. The bark is thick and soft, the floor is dry. I sit in the hollow with my mate. The floor is warm, the walls are damp. I can hear the wind through the branches, and the leaves fall in the night. The hollow is mine, and the marsh is mine, and the pond is mine.

The hollow in the old beech, dark and dry, where I roost. I sit on a branch above the floor, the floor is the earth. The wood is soft and the wind moves through it, like a voice. I can hear the hollow from a mile away.

My hollow in the old beech, three feet from the ground. The bark is rough and cold. The wood is dry and soft. I have a hollow in each side, and the floor is covered with leaves and the old pellets I have not eaten. It is warm and safe. I have been here for twenty winters.

A hollow in an old beech, high in the wood, the bark rough and the leaves thin. A dry floor, a soft bed of leaves, a warm hollow in the trunk. I have been here since the wind first howled through the beeches. I know every crack in the bark, every shadow in the hollow. I sleep in it, I rest in it, I watch from it.
